$comment: Day 53 (Phase 4c step 5.1): dated trade routes for the globe. points are [lat, lng] waypoints (sea lanes stay off the coast). See docs/DATA.md.

routes.name: Silk Roads
routes.goods: Silk, paper, porcelain, horses, glass, silver, spices; also Buddhism, Islam, paper-making and plague
routes.description: Not one road but a web of caravan tracks between China and the Mediterranean. Han envoy Zhang Qian's missions (from c. 138 BCE) opened regular contact, and goods moved in relays from oasis to oasis: few merchants ever walked the whole way. Traffic rose and fell with the empires along it (Han, Kushan, Parthian, Tang, Abbasid, Mongol) and faded as sea routes took over in the 15th century.

confidence.reason: The oasis cities are well known; the tracks between them shifted with wars, water and rulers, so the lines follow the main corridors.

routes.name: Indian Ocean monsoon trade
routes.goods: Pepper, cotton cloth, gems, ivory, gold, incense, horses, porcelain, enslaved people
routes.description: Sailors timed their voyages to the monsoon: south-west winds carried ships towards India in summer and north-east winds brought them back in winter. Greek and Roman merchants learned the open-sea crossing from Egypt to India around the 1st century BCE (the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea is their handbook), but Arab, Persian, Indian, Malay, Chinese and Swahili traders ran the network for centuries. Portuguese fleets forced their way in after 1498.

confidence.reason: Ports and seasonal winds are well documented; the open-sea lanes drawn here are typical tracks, not logged courses.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea

routes.name: Trans-Saharan caravans
routes.goods: West African gold, Saharan salt, copper, cloth, books, horses, enslaved people
routes.description: Camel caravans, some of a thousand animals or more, crossed the Sahara between the Maghreb and the cities of the Sahel. Gold from West Africa went north and salt from mines like Taghaza went south, making Ghana, Mali and Songhai rich and carrying Islam and scholarship to Timbuktu. Trade crossed the desert long before, but its peak ran from the 8th to the early 17th century, after which Atlantic shipping drew trade to the coast.

confidence.reason: Termini and oases are known from Arab geographers and travellers such as Ibn Battuta; the desert tracks between them are drawn as straight-ish lines.

routes.name: Amber Road
routes.goods: Baltic amber; in return Roman coins, bronze, glass and wine
routes.description: Amber, 'the gold of the north', had travelled south from the Baltic for thousands of years. Under Rome the trade ran along a road from Aquileia on the Adriatic through Carnuntum on the Danube and the Moravian Gate to the Baltic coast; Pliny tells of a knight sent north under Nero who came back with tons of it.

confidence.reason: The Roman stretch from Aquileia to Carnuntum follows known towns; the route north of the Danube is reconstructed from finds of amber and coins.

routes.name: Hanseatic League
routes.goods: Grain, timber, furs, wax, salted herring, stockfish, cloth, salt, beer
routes.description: A league of merchant towns, led by Lübeck, that dominated trade on the North Sea and the Baltic. Its four great foreign offices (Kontors) were the Steelyard in London, Bruges, Bergen and the Peterhof in Novgorod. Herring, Norwegian stockfish, Russian furs and Baltic grain moved west; cloth, salt and silver moved east. The last Hanseatic diet met in 1669.

confidence.reason: Member towns and Kontors are documented; the sea lanes drawn between them are typical coastal routes.

routes.name: Manila galleons
routes.goods: Chinese silk and porcelain, spices and ivory east; Mexican and Peruvian silver west
routes.description: For 250 years, one or two Spanish galleons a year crossed the Pacific between Manila and Acapulco. Westbound they ran with the trade winds past Guam; eastbound, after Andrés de Urdaneta found the return route in 1565, they rode the Kuroshio and the westerlies far north before turning down the California coast, a voyage of four to six months. American silver bought Chinese goods in Manila, tying Asia, the Americas and Europe into one trade.

confidence.reason: Sailing dates, ports and the usual courses are recorded in Spanish logs; each voyage drifted a little from the track drawn.

routes.name: Atlantic triangular trade
routes.goods: European guns, cloth and metalware to Africa; enslaved Africans to the Americas; sugar, tobacco, cotton and rum to Europe
routes.description: Ships left European ports with manufactured goods, bought enslaved people on the West and West-Central African coast, carried them across the Atlantic (the Middle Passage) and returned with plantation goods. About 12.5 million Africans were forced aboard and some 1.8 million died on the crossing. Many voyages were not triangles at all: the largest single flow was direct between Brazil and Angola. The trade was abolished nation by nation; the last known voyages reached Cuba in the 1860s.

confidence.reason: Ports and voyage counts are well documented (the Slave Voyages database); the ocean legs drawn here are typical tracks.
